newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania protests roll on, Berisha seeks support.
newsitem.headline: Albania protests roll on, Berisha seeks support.

text.p: Albanian President Sali Berisha campaigned hard to woo back the support of an impoverished people but a wave of anti-government mass protests rolled on unabated in the southern port of Vlore.

About 8,000 demonstrators marched through Vlore on Friday for a 17th day to demand the government's resignation and compensation for life savings lost when a string of fraudulent pyramid funds collapsed in January.

A group of some 60 Vlore students who have gone on hunger strike issued a petition asking foreign governments to step up pressure on Albania's rulers to quit and urging students across the Balkans to join their protest.
Scores of children and women led the demonstrators who converged at nightfall in front of the university building to express solidarity with the hunger strikers inside.
"We want the money of our parents back," read a banner carried by a young girl escorted by her mother.

Five weeks of protests and violent unrest across the country have posed the most serious challenge to the five-year rule of Berisha and the right-wing Democratic Party government of Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi.

Berisha on Friday kept up his week-long campaign to tell Albanians the government would do all it could to help ease their plight. He has promised to speed up growth and exempt hard-hit investors from paying taxes for two years.
After holding a series of speeches in the capital Tirana and the towns of Lushnje and Elbasan over the past days, he travelled to Peshkopi in Albania's rugged north-east.
Berisha was expected to take his election-style campaign to Shkoder, 180 km (110 miles) north of Tirana, on Saturday.
"Only the Democratic Party can offer the best solution in this situation," he told told a crowd of about 5,000 before adressing some 1,500 party faithfuls in Peshkopi's theatre.
Berisha has admitted that he made some mistakes over the past years, but has steadfastly stood behind his government.
He told supporters that a group of 14 Democratic Party MP's which had demanded Meksi's resignation wanted to destabilise the country and team up with the Socialist opposition.
"To those who suggest a government with the Socialists I say right here: Your red dreams will never come true," he said.
Meksi himself has denied that his ruling Democrats were split, telling critics who sought his resignation they were free to leave the party.
"They have a right to their opinion and they have the right not to stay with us at this difficult moment," he told Reuters.

Destitute investors blame the government for failing to reign in the schemes, which used new money to cover sky-high interest rates due on older deposits. An estimated $1 to $2 billion was sunk in such funds, some economists estimate.
The growth of the schemes has dealt a heavy blow to the fledgling market economy which has emerged in Europe's poorest nation since its hardline Stalinist regime fell in 1990.
The government now faces the uneasy choice of printing money to appease angry investors, dealing a potentially fatal blow to Albania's frail economy, or standing firm and risking more social turmoil.
